lead: The combustion chamber is the space above the piston at TDC, where the charge burns. Its shape decides how fast the charge burns, how much heat leaks into the walls, whether the end gas knocks, how well the engine breathes and, in a diesel, how well the fuel meets the air. SI engines use compact shapes with a central plug, such as the hemispherical, pent-roof, wedge and bathtub heads. CI engines use either an open chamber with a bowl in the piston (direct injection) or a divided chamber with a small pre-chamber (indirect injection).
prereq: You need: knock and its factors (factors affecting knock), the CI delay (CI combustion) and air motion (swirl, squish and tumble).

blocks.text: The chamber volume at TDC is the clearance volume Vc, and any bowl or pre-chamber is part of it. Compression ratio r = (Vs + Vc) ÷ Vc, where Vs is the swept volume. Every design balances these objectives:

items: High volumetric efficiency: room for large valves and smooth ports.
Short flame path and fast burn: a compact chamber with the plug near the centre (SI); good spray–air matching (CI).
High anti-knock quality (SI): the end gas kept small, cool and close to a cooled wall, often in a squish band.
Low surface-to-volume ratio: less wall area means less heat loss and fewer flame-quench layers that leave unburnt hydrocarbons.
No hot spots: the exhaust valve and plug well cooled, no sharp edges.
Controlled turbulence: enough squish, swirl or tumble for a fast burn, but not so much that heat loss soars.

Hemispherical: a dome-shaped head with inclined valves on both sides and a central plug. Short flame path, large valves and good breathing, and the lowest surface-to-volume ratio of the common shapes, so heat loss is low and high compression ratios suit it. It gives little squish, and the valve gear is complex and costly.
Pent-roof: the modern four-valve version of the hemispherical idea, with two flat roof faces, the plug in the middle and strong tumble from the steep inlet ports.

Wedge: valves in a line, inclined; the thin end of the wedge forms a squish area that keeps the end gas cool and adds turbulence. Cheap and knock-resistant, but the flame path from a plug at the thick end is longer.
Bathtub: an oval recess in a flat head with vertical in-line valves and squish areas on both sides. Simple and cheap, with good squish, but the valves are small, so breathing is weaker.

blocks.text: Older layouts (the side-valve L-head and T-head) had long flame paths and large surfaces; they survive only in textbooks and small stationary engines.

sections.h3: CI chambers: direct and indirect injection

blocks.text: Direct injection (DI), open chambers. Fuel is sprayed straight into a bowl in the piston crown through a central multi-hole nozzle at high pressure. Variants: a shallow open (quiescent) chamber for large slow engines, where the sprays do the mixing; and deep bowls, such as hemispherical, cylindrical and toroidal or re-entrant bowls, which use swirl and squish for mixing in smaller, faster engines. DI gives the best fuel economy and easy cold starting, because the chamber surface is small, but it needs high injection pressure, a high-cetane fuel and careful spray–bowl matching, and it is louder.

Indirect injection (IDI), divided chambers. Fuel is sprayed into a small chamber in the head joined to the main chamber by a throat. In a swirl chamber (such as the Ricardo Comet) the air is forced in through a tangential throat during compression and swirls hard; in a pre-combustion chamber the burning starts in the small chamber and a jet of burning gas blasts into the main chamber; air-cell and energy-cell designs work on the same idea. IDI needs only a single-hole pintle nozzle at low pressure, runs smoothly and quietly, tolerates poorer fuel and reaches high speeds. But the extra surface and throat losses waste heat, so fuel economy is 10 to 15 % worse than DI and a glow plug is needed for cold starting.

Factors that shape the design: bore (flame path and spray length), compression ratio (knock in SI, cold start in CI), valve size and number (two valves push the plug or injector off-centre), injector position and spray angle, cooling of the exhaust side, and cost.

examples.question: A DI diesel has bore 100 mm and stroke 110 mm. Its piston bowl is 60 mm across and 16 mm deep (take it as a cylinder). The squish gap at TDC is 1.0 mm over the full bore, and valve cut-outs and crevices add 0.90 cm³. Find the clearance volume, the compression ratio and the share of the clearance volume held by the bowl.
steps: Bore area = (π/4) × 10² = 78.54 cm². Swept volume V<sub>s</sub> = 78.54 × 11.0 = 863.9 cm³.
examples.answer: V<sub>c</sub> = 54.0 cm³ and r = 17.0; the bowl holds about 84 % of the clearance volume, which is why nearly all the air is in the bowl, swirling, when the fuel arrives.

examples.question: An SI engine has bore 86 mm and clearance volume 62.44 cm³. Compare the surface-to-volume ratio of (a) a flat disc chamber between a flat head and a flat piston and (b) a dome (spherical cap) over a flat piston, both of 62.44 cm³.
steps: (b) A cap of base radius a = 4.3 cm and height h has V = πh(3a² + h²)/6. Setting V = 62.44 cm³ and solving gives h = 2.00 cm (check: π × 2.00 × (55.47 + 4.02)/6 = 62.3 ≈ 62.44 cm³).
The dome has 11 % less surface for the same volume.
examples.answer: (a) 2.33 cm⁻¹. (b) 2.06 cm⁻¹. The dome loses less heat and has less quench area, one reason hemispherical and pent-roof heads burn efficiently.

traps: The hemispherical chamber has the lowest surface-to-volume ratio of the common SI shapes, so low heat loss; its weak point is little squish, not a large surface.
A pre-chamber or swirl-chamber engine is indirect injection; direct injection sprays into a bowl in the piston.
The bowl is part of the clearance volume; do not add it again when finding the compression ratio.
IDI runs quieter and tolerates poor fuel, but DI gives the better fuel economy and cold starting.
Convert bowl depth from mm to cm before working in cm³.

quiz.q: List four objectives of SI combustion chamber design.
quiz.a: Any four: high volumetric efficiency, short flame path, high anti-knock quality, low surface-to-volume ratio, no hot spots, controlled turbulence.

quiz.q: Name two DI and two IDI diesel chamber types.
quiz.a: DI: shallow open (quiescent) chamber, toroidal or re-entrant bowl (also hemispherical, cylindrical). IDI: swirl chamber (Ricardo Comet), pre-combustion chamber (also air cell, energy cell).

quiz.q: Why does a hemispherical head breathe well but burn slowly at part load?
quiz.a: Inclined valves on both sides can be large, so volumetric efficiency is high; but it has almost no squish, so turbulence is low and the flame is slower at part load.

quiz.q: Why is an IDI diesel less efficient than a DI diesel?
quiz.a: The pre-chamber and throat add wall area and throttling losses, so more heat is lost; a DI chamber is compact with less surface.

quiz.q: A DI bowl is 60 mm across and 15 mm deep; the clearance volume is 65 cm³. Find the bowl volume and its share.
A diesel has V<sub>s</sub> = 500 cm³ and r = 18. Find V<sub>c</sub>.
Choose a DI or IDI diesel for a small generator in a village with variable fuel quality, and for a long-haul truck. Justify.
quiz.a: Generator: IDI, which tolerates poorer fuel, is simple, quiet and needs only low injection pressure. Truck: DI, for 10 to 15 % better fuel economy and easy starting, with good fuel and a high-pressure injection system.

quiz.q: Why do large-bore petrol engines use two plugs or a central plug?
quiz.a: The flame path grows with bore, so the end gas waits longer and knock risk rises; a central plug or two plugs shortens the path.

beyond: Car diesels have all moved to DI with common rail and re-entrant bowls shaped in CFD; IDI survives in some small engines. Petrol engines use pent-roof heads with tumble ports, and some use small jet-ignition pre-chambers for very lean running. Search for re-entrant bowl design, pent-roof chamber and pre-chamber jet ignition.

figure.caption: Four chamber types in section. The SI shapes keep the flame path short; the DI diesel holds most of its clearance volume in the piston bowl (84 % in the worked example); the IDI diesel burns first in a swirl chamber joined by a throat.

spec.aria: Four section sketches. Hemispherical SI chamber: a dome with a central plug and inclined valves, surface to volume ratio 2.06 per centimetre. Wedge SI chamber: a sloping head with the plug at the thick end and a squish arrow at the thin end. Direct injection diesel: a central injector spraying into a 60 by 16 millimetre bowl in the piston, compression ratio 17. Indirect injection diesel: a round swirl chamber in the head with a pintle nozzle, joined to the main chamber by a throat.
